paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: what you value shows up in what you trade it for. Esau comes in famished and says, "I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?" (Genesis 25:32). I think the hunger was loud and the birthright was quiet, so the loud thing won. Then the text gives its verdict: "Thus Esau despised his birthright." (Genesis 25:34).

Now look at how this passage starts. Rebekah doesn't understand what's happening inside her, so she goes to inquire of the LORD, and He tells her, "the older will serve the younger." (Genesis 25:22-23). Isaac prays for his wife, and the LORD hears him (Genesis 25:21). This family is not running on luck. God is already speaking and already at work before either boy takes a breath, and Esau's hunger doesn't change that.

So here's what I want you to carry out of my bakery. Everybody gets famished. A rough day, a loud craving, a moment that says "right now matters more than anything." Before that moment comes, decide what is precious to you, and bring your questions to the LORD like Rebekah did, because a hungry baker will sell the whole bakery for one warm cookie. And this family's story? It's only getting started.
